utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Gotovina, et al. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today a hearing was scheduled mainly with the purpose to find out where we stand with the requested documents, documents requested by the Prosecution. The Prosecution had then sought an order under Rule 54 and where the Chamber has instructed Croatia to further explore and do further research to see what could be find or not. And at this moment we have a list of documents which were not produced, and we have a list of documents that were produced. And most important for the Chamber is find out where we are, where there is disagreement, what kind of disagreement there is, so as to know how the Chamber should proceed in relation to this order. In order to avoid any misunderstanding, this is not a hearing in which the Chamber seeks evidence on how it was at the time and what command structures were there, et cetera. Evidence is led by the parties. The Chamber will consider that. The focus is on where we stand with the production of documents. For that purpose, we have invited the Republic of Croatia to attend, and I would like to invite the representatives of the Republic of Croatia to introduce themselves. Who will introduce the members of the delegation which appears before the Chamber today? Could the one who speaks start with introducing himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARKOTIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. My name is Gordan Markotic, head of directorate for cooperation with the International Criminal Courts of the Ministry of Justice of Croatia. With me today to my right is Mr. Ivan Crncec, head of department within the Ministry of Justice. Next, Mr. Drazen Keser, Colonel Minister of Defence. Next to him is Mr. Zeljko Sklepic also a Colonel from the Ministry of Defence. In the second row, to my left, Ms. Zeljka Pokupec, Zagreb Municipal Prosecutor. Next to her, Mr. -- excuse me, Josip Cule, Deputy State Prosecutor. And next to him, Mr. Vitomir Bijelic, head of crime police of the Ministry of Interior. That is our delegation of today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Markotic, for introducing the delegation members. Just for you to know, but you may be aware of it already, that the Prosecution is sitting to your left, and, at the other side of this courtroom we'll find the Defence teams. Back row, is, at this moment, Gotovina Defence; middle row is the Cermak Defence; and front row is the Markac Defence. And the seating is more or less a consequence of the stage of the proceedings, in which we are at this moment. That is, that the Markac Defence is presenting its Defence case. I take it that you know counsel. Mr. Mikulicic, who is now looking at me. Perhaps if you raise your hand, Mr. Mikulicic, to the extend you're not known.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Here I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, Mr. Kuzmanovic, seated here. Mr. Kay in the middle row. At the back row, Mr. Kehoe and Mr. Misetic. The Prosecution is represented today, front row, Mr. Tieger, Ms. Gustafson, and in the back I see Mr. Waespi present. So now we all know each other. This is the Bench as you are now aware of. I would like to put on the record that the latest report was received, I think, yesterday. It is in B/C/S. It is a report of approximately 140 pages. It has not been translated yet, so, therefore, whatever is in there, the Chamber doesn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With regard to the production yesterday of 140 pages, I don't believe the parties have gotten that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check. I think the Chamber received that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, I think we received an original copy yesterday, and I remember there was an issue about you receiving only in December a report which was produced in November, and I took it that this was the result of it not yet being translated. Now, I do understand that members of your team can read the original language. At the same time, the Prosecution asked for those reports, and if it receives it, I can imagine that they want to know what they received before distributing it, because they have asked for it. Now, Mr. Tieger, at this moment, I see now three persons on their feet. Could you give us further information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to what I believe to be the report that's referenced, I was handed a hard copy of that this morning in court about five or ten minutes before the proceeding commenced. I understand that arrived in our office sometime late yesterday afternoon. And that's all I know about it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I mean, obviously with this hearing and to be of some meaningful response to anything that the Republic of Croatia is going to say, of course, my colleague Mr. Misetic speaks the language, and he can be of assistance if we could have a copy now so that he could peruse even as we speak, which I'm sure that the Prosecution is doing at this juncture. It may be beneficial as we move through this session today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We received yesterday a copy: Report on the documents concerning Operations Flash and Storm for the attention of Trial Chamber I. Mr. Tieger, is there any problem if the Defence would receive a copy? Or, otherwise, I mean, if we would received it tomorrow, we would have had the meeting today as well. As soon as anyone starts referring to it, we will find a procedural solution for that. It seems that we could never have a hearing because it is an ongoing stream of reports which reaches us, and I'm not criticising receiving reports because the Chamber ordered to do it -- the Republic of Croatia to its utmost best to -- well, to research what can be found, what could not be found and to report to -- also what has been done in order to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The only reason I raise the issue, Mr. President, is, of course, we have read the submission by the Republic of Croatia that came in, in November that we received last week. And as we go through it factually, we -- there are significant issues that I'm sure at some juncture if it becomes an issue you might turn to the parties and say, Is this correct? And I would say, Mr. President, it is not correct. So that is because we have had that opportunity. And all I'm saying is as we move through this, if there is some reference to this document, it just may be of assistance to give to Mr. Misetic for him to review as we go through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, would there be any problem in providing a copy to Mr. Misetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mean procedurally or logistically, Your Honour? I'm not aware of any reason --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Logistically, I take it -- I mean, copies are there. It takes five minutes to photocopy it. Procedurally?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of any, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you wouldn't mind if a copy would be given to Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It will assist our Defence team as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I will ask any more -- Mr. Kay, you start reading B/C/S as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Obviously if there could be some material in there, I would like to see the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I will ask the Registry, and we will proceed on a basis of a lack of knowledge of this document, apart from that you know approximately how thick it is. That's all we know at this moment and that it has been apparently delivered on the -- it has been sent, I see, on the 14th of December, to the ICTY Liaison Office. And I can already tell you four documents are provided: An order dated the 16th of June, 1998; an order dated the 25th of June, also 1998; a memo on delivery of documents dated the 27th of August, 1998; a memo on the collecting of documents dated the 23rd of November, 1998. And apparently there was a report, the implementation plan. The report on the completion of activities of the task force after the submitted report, dated the 9th of November. Apparently there is an follow-up report. The tabular survey of activities and a list of Official Notes regarding the interviews conducted with ... and then follows a list of 32 names, and apparently the Official Notes are in the Croatian language only at this moment. That is what you could expect once it has been photocopied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Filing of the document may take quite a while, because the major parts are not translated yet. You'll receive an electronic copy, if that is okay with you, so that can you look at it on your screen. Mr. Kay, if you have any difficulties with that, the Chamber will assist you. Then the Chamber has received voluminous material over the last year. The Chamber should keep an eye on whether the Government of Croatia, whether the Republic of Croatia, fulfils its duties under the Statute and under the orders given by the Chamber. The Chamber does not consider it its task to go through all these material which is provided primarily to report to the Prosecution what documents have been found and what reasons are given for not finding them, or what has been done, in order to try to find them. For transparency purposes the Chamber considers it not appropriate that we are going through every detail of all the material we have because that might blur the view of the parties on what the Chamber has digested in hearing this case. Therefore the Chamber will primarily focus on the discussion between the parties; that is, what has been provided, is there an explanation for the non-existence of certain documents which were not provided. And we might not go through the whole list, but the Chamber would like to engage in an exercise to find out where we stand at this moment in relation to the production of these documents and where, apparently, difficulties are found. And I'd like to start with that at this moment. We will use the numbering of the initial request. We have a long list of documents the Prosecution was seeking. There were 328 documents the Prosecution were seeking. Quite a few of them in various copies. If we are talking about single copies, that is, every document in only one version, not several copies, I think we were talking about 158 documents which we find in the Appendix C to the Prosecution's application for an order, pursuant to Rule 54 bis. I'll refer to these numbers as the numbers of the original list. Of course, there are other filings of a later date, and especially important, I would say is, Appendix A to the Prosecution's response to Croatia's 2nd of June, 2009 request, filed on the 19th of June. I would call that the Prosecution's latest list in which we see that 63 documents remain to be found. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. One point of clarification at this point, and that is we're talking about 150 -- when you mentioned the 158 and the remaining documents that are at -- they're identified in various filings, we're talking about categories of documents the parties have agreed; that is, I should say, parties that -- in discussions with Croatia it's clear that any number of those categories may have been produced with numerous documents. That will be raised during the course of the hearing as well. So just to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Appendix B, also filed on the 19th of June, refers to a report by Croatia on the 24th of April, 2009, which is also an important document for orientation for this Chamber. Finally, we have Attachment 2 to Croatia's report of the 29th of September, which is important, but I'll not go through all of the filings. It's just for your information that we have considered that, and we also have considered the Prosecution's submission of received artillery documents which were filed on the 7th of December. That's a little bit over a week ago, which has its own numbering. And, as I said before, we have not looked at the latest filing which was received yesterday. What I would like to do is to go through some of these documents, to find out where we are, whether certain documents are still sought, or whether the explanation given by the Republic of Croatia is accepted by the Prosecution, and, of course, whatever else any of the parties would like to raise in this respect, the parties are free to raise that. If there are any further comments by the Republic of Croatia, that is fine. But this is not an evidentiary hearing, so what happened at the time, et cetera, we are talking about what explains why documents were produced or were not produced and what keeps the parties and what keeps the Republic of Croatia and the Prosecution apart, and perhaps also the other -- the other -- the Defence teams, in accepting each other's explanations for the present situation. I would therefore like to start with a focus on - and I'm now referring to the original list - 68, 69, 78, 79, 88, 89. The request was about regular reports from TRS-1 to Operational Group North. One of the issues that arises in relation to these documents, and you see that we have three couples, 68, 69 regular reports, 4th of August, 1995. 78, 79; 5th of August. 88, 89; 6th of August. Six documents were requested; that is, a.m. reports and p.m. reports for each of these days. The Republic of Croatia has reported that only one daily report was produced and that this is supported by -- for example, the numbering of those documents. So the first question that arises may be whether the Prosecution accepts the explanation that only one report, regular report, TRS-1 to Operational Group North was produced on those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Well, in the spirit of consensus I see you focused on appropriate categories of documents, and the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I grouped them to some extent together, because these are reports sought of a similar kind for the various dates, and we'll do that often that we group together reports 4th, 5th, and 6th of August because the explanations often are of a similar kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I mentioned consensus because that's precisely what exists with respect to these reports. The Prosecution agrees with the interpretation of the officials of the authorities of the Republic of Croatia. The backdrop to this consensus is that with respect to those documents there was originally a response from the Republic of Croatia that the -- those particular documents would not be found in the central military archive because they had an HVO origin. We then advised the Croatian authorities that there was information that the Croatian state archive in Zagreb contained such documents. Documents were thereafter produced which validated the interpretation indicated that reports were produced once a day, rather than twice. And on that basis, we agree with the position with respect to the documents the Court just identified, and there is no dispute between the -- between the Republic of Croatia and the Prosecution on those categories of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, we can strike from the list half of these numbers. There's no dispute about them anymore. One being produced means the second for that day has become moot.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's correct, so the -- that's correct. Where, as previously, the request was for documents produced twice a day, with respect to these categories, we agree that they were produced the once a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And we find them in the filing of the 7th of December. The documents that the OTP received from Croatia under the numbers -- and there we have a different numbering. 15, 18, and 21, where we find documents with sequential numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This might be typical for today that everyone has to check whether what has been said is accurate or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore 68, 69, 78, 79, 88, 89, three reports have been received; the other three can be stricken from the list as still being sought. Now often the reporting is in one way or another related to ordering. Could I ask your specific attention for the report of the 4th of August with the number the UR number 1714-VI/0195128.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, you previously identified --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's number 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Number 15 on the report filed on the ... Among these reports -- Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, is it number 15 in Annex C of 2008?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it is number 15 in the filing of documents the OTP received from Croatia which were filed the 7th of December, 2009. It's dated the 4th of August, although there is an illegible stamp on it, 5th of August. That's at least what I see in my ... Yes, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm just trying to -- Mr. Misetic and I are just trying to get on the same page with the Chamber. The report that we have filed by Office of the Prosecutor on 4 December for 15, in my sheet and Mr. Misetic's sheet, says regular report from TRS-1 to OG North. Am I mistaken in looking at the wrong document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I thought you just mentioned an attack order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I said that this reporting sometimes is related to orders given, and that is a matter I would briefly explore, not in full detail, but -- Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I -- I think I understand Mr. Kehoe's reference, and I believe he is focussing momentarily on attack order because of number 15. That's -- I believe he may have turned to number 15 in the Appendix C -- okay. Because that would have reflected an attack order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, I'm talking about a document which was signed and stamped by Stipo Gotovac. Mr. Tieger in this document, and it's one of the three documents we just referred to -- yes, Mr. Markotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARKOTIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. We cannot follow your discussion because we don't have an OTP list. You are mentioning a OTP list dated the 7th of December, 2009. We can only follow Annex C, so we don't what this is all about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would -- we are still talking about the document 68, 69 of the original list. And I have seen that in the response Croatia has used the numbering of the original list when commenting on matters, and that's the documents we are talking about. Is that clear? So among the three groups of two, 68, 69, 78, 79, 88, 89, there is no problem anymore whether what was produced is everything that was asked for. Now, Mr. Tieger, in the report for the -- dated the 4th of August, reference is made to an order of the commander of the TG ZP, dated the 3rd of August. Is that a document which was sought, and/or produced? Because the Chamber understands that in line of analysing what the Prosecution sought is always a combination of who gave orders to what and what was reported back. Now, in the other of these documents, we find no reference to - and I'm now talking about again the regular reports, TRS-1 for the 4th, the 5th, and the 6th of August - we find no reference to any previous orders; it's just a report. Now here there is a specific reference to an order apparently relevant for the report to be sent. The Chamber wondered whether that's any of the orders that were sought and/or produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, again when you say "any of the orders," Your Honour, I don't want to expand us beyond Appendix C for the moment. I don't believe that is one of the categories in Appendix C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Which I understood to be the Court's question, so I wanted to make it clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because it's quite an exercise to always link the one list to another. Okay. Then as far as the Chamber is concerned we have done with the series, 68, 69, 78, 79, 88, 89. And then I would like to move to the next series. If any of the parties would like to make any further submissions in relation to these documents, they're invited to do so now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, on behalf of the Gotovina Defence, we have just a general position with respect to all of the TRS-1 and TRS-2 documents. I won't pull it up, but I would draw the court's attention to D971, and it gives you where these groups actually operated on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Under Rule 54 bis, (A) subpart (ii), there is a requirement for the party moving under 54 bis to indicate how the document is relevant to any matter in issue before the Judge or Trial Chamber and necessary for a fair determination of that matter. So there is a necessity element in the Rule. Just generally speaking, Mr. President, I won't take the position that there's no relevance to TRS-2 and TRS-1; however, we would question how material these documents are to any issues that are in dispute in this case, which, of course, this indictment concerns only events that took place on the territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's on the record. That may come back in relation to one of the other documents, because, apparently, here, there seems to be no remaining problem. Then -- thank you, Mr. Misetic, for this submission. Then I would like to move to the next series, which is 70, 71, 80, 81, 90, 91, which are regular reports from TRS-2 to Operational Group North for, respectively, the 4th, the 5th, and the 6th of August, 1995. If we look at the positions by the Republic of Croatia and the Prosecution in this respect, I would like to draw your attention to Appendix B to the OTP response to the request of Republic of Croatia, dated the 2nd June of 2009, which was filed on the 19th of June. We find here the position of Croatia, that, according to the statement of Ante Kardum, he went each night to the meetings at the Operational Group command, where all the commanders subordinated to that Operational Group delivered reports and that he did so as well. That he presented his reports on activities, balance and consumption of ammunition from the agenda in which he had written information he received from his subordinates. And Mr. Kardum claims that he has never kept any diaries or wrote reports, except occasionally in extraordinary circumstances when someone was killed, et cetera. The Prosecution states that Kardum's statement is in contradiction with Rajcic's statement, in which he said that he had compiled written reports. The Chamber would like to hear further submissions of the parties on acceptance or non-acceptance of this explanation by the Republic of Croatia or a further explanation of the exact contradiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was mixing up matters which I should not have done. We'll come to the other, the Kardum/Rajcic contradiction. We come to that later. And I resume the position taken by the Republic of Croatia, and forget about what I said before, in relation to 70 and 71. The position was that the documents requested were supposed to have been drafted as requested. That's how it started. Apparently here also is a morning, afternoon discussion, whether there were two reports or one report on the same day, but since none of the reports has been produced we cannot rely on any sequential numbering of reports. The statement of the reasons given by Croatia is that TRS-2, as an element of the corps artillery, provided artillery support to the HVO units under the command of Brigadier Zeljko Glasnovic from the HVO, from the IZM OG North in the village of Vrba on the auxiliary axis of attack, and they should have submitted their reports to that command. In the response to the Prosecution's motion, the Prosecution then objected that Croatia had failed to ask Rahim Ademi on the existence of those document, referring to Rajcic, who stated that generally groups were supposed to compile reports twice a day. In response to that, the Republic of Croatia said that an interview with the commander of TRS-2, Tomislav Alajica, was re-done, who does not give a pre-emptory reply is in a statement whether he was compiling written daily reports. Reference is made to a statement by Alajica in footnote 50, a statement of the 2nd of February, 2009. We did not find any Alajica statements in the earlier submissions. However, there is a statement in the December series, to say so, the recently translated and filed reports, but that is a statement not of the 2nd of February, 2009, but a statement of the 24th of October of 2009. The -- apparently Croatia says, We have to final answer it. The question may be, Why not, if he doesn't give a pre-emptory answer? What to do under those circumstances. And I would like to hear the positions of the Prosecution and the position of the Republic of Croatia in this respect. And if there's any reason to rely on the 24th of October, 2009, statement, the Chamber would like to hear exactly what portions are relevant for the answer to this dispute. Perhaps I first give an opportunity to the Republic of Croatia. And I also draw your attention to -- no, that's a different matter. No, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARKOTIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Colonel Keser will respond to this issue, and by your leave, I would like to turn the floor to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KESER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, concerning the issue of the reports of the TRS-2, which are the subject of this request, we can state that during an interview with the commander of that group whose name is Tomislav Alajica we ascertained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I stop you for a second. If you're referring to any interview, could you give us the date of that interview because we have apparently several dates for interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. KESER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am referring to the interview of the 2nd of February, 2009.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KESER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that interview, Commander Alajica reported that he did not draft written reports about the activities of his artillery rocket group. He stated that he reported orally to Brigadier Glasnovic in the village of Vrba by phone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is anything further said in what appears to be a more recent interview with Mr. Alajica? Again, the Chamber has not searched all the boxes to find its own evidential material for taking positions. It's exactly the reason why we have this hearing, that we would like to hear from the parties. Mr. Tieger, the position of the Prosecution in relation to these reports, do you accept oral reporting by telephone on these dates? Are there reasons to challenge that explanation?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the -- with respect to the February 2nd interview, the only reference to communications with Glasnovic occurs in the fourth paragraph. Well there's -- first, there's an initial reference to the fact -- to him. And then it indicates, After taking up positions he contacted Glasnovic and got further instructions and a list of possible targets. There was reference to the absence of a pre-emptory response. The Prosecution's position is that this question was not resolved by the single reference to Glasnovic in that interview or at least any other reference that I can find. And neither in this interview or the later interview was the matter directly taken up with a Alajica. And for that matter, unlike the previous position which was resolved through the existing reports, the sequential numbering, we cannot agree that this issue has been resolved by this interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do then understand that the Prosecution takes that the reference in the February interview was rather vague and, as it was reported by the Republic of Croatia, that it was not a pre-emptory reply. Now, since Mr. Alajica has been further interviewed on the 24th of October, and, again, it's not the task of this Chamber to find the sources without being guided by the parties on this matter. Has an attempt been made in the 24th of October to further clarify the issue of reporting where the Republic of Croatia itself said that Mr. Alajica had not provided a pre-emptory reply? I see that the new statement, the new interview, dated the 24th of October, 2009, has been filed by the Prosecution in its filing on the 9th of December. Could the Republic of Croatia point at any specific part in this interview which would shed further light on this matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, where I said "filed by the Prosecution," I meant to say reported a month before by the Republic of Croatia. Is there any portion of this interview which sheds further light on this matter? Who takes the floor?

utterances.speaker: MR. CRNCEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the interview concerned does not contain such data. However, we would like to point out the interview with Drazen Vukelja, dated the 13th of February, 2009. He was also a member of the TRS-2. He states that he cannot remember seeing Commander Alajica writing any reports. However, he does recall that when Alajica went to briefings at the command, that it was Vukelja who personally told him which orders were received on that particular day, whether there were any activities undertaken, and the amount of ammunition spent. He also shared with him the time of operation, as well as the targets. Alajica, in turn, wrote that down in his notebook, and briefed accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Has the Prosecution considered this statement in still challenging the claimed non-existence of written reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, to my knowledge that wasn't the subject of direct discussions with the Republic of Croatia, but I don't believe it resolves the issue, first of all. To the extent there's a suggestion that there's a causal connection between the briefings and the -- any information provided by Vukelja, I don't think that's warranted in the Official Note, but in any event, they're of such a nature you would be hard-pressed to make that direct contention one way or another since it is relatively subtle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would say it is marginal information for the core of the dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right, and I further say the fact that when oral information is being transmitted, it is immediately written down, overall supports the Prosecution's position throughout that these important matters weren't simply communicated orally but, were memorialised in various way, including reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You referred to an interview with Mr. Vukelja February 2009. Now, there is another interview held with him on the 24th of October 2009. Does that interview shed any further light, whether positive or negative, on the issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. CRNCEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. In that interview, there's no mention of that particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Crncec. The Official Notes of the interviews have been filed, as far as the October interviews are concerned. Could the parties, could you, Mr. Tieger, or could you assist us in where to find the February interviews, both of Mr. Alajica, and of Mr. -- let me -- Mr. Vukelja. Where does the Chamber find them? Again, we have not gone through every little piece of paper in those boxes for the reasons I stated before, but if there is anything in which we'll find a clue for resolving matters which apparently still are in dispute, we would like to be informed about the specific sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, of course, we're more than happy to file these if they haven't been. I would note that the -- our June 2009 submission was accompanied by the interviews which were referred to in that submission. So I can't say with certainty that this one is in that submission. And in fact I'm advised that -- that it is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have -- I have Official Notes, Appendix C to the response which was filed on the 19th of June. The Official Notes of interviews with Mr. Kardum, First, Ivanovic, Kotromanovic, Glavan, Ragulj, Bagic, and Gotovac. I have no others. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How to proceed in respect of this apparent point of dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, as I say, with respect to the interviews, we're more than happy to make those available to the Court. The Court has heard them discussed, so you will have an opportunity to peruse them on your own. I would note one further matter with respect to the -- to that particular issue and the reliance or non-reliance on the Vukelja interview, and I would turn the court's attention to the information derived from interviews with Mr. Rajcic who asserted that reports from TRS-2 were, indeed, received. So that is another factor that bears on the Prosecution's position with respect to whether the Alajica or Vukelja interviews resolve this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I suggest that, after this hearing, on the matters we have specifically discussed and which have not been resolved, that we -- that the parties will file primarily, perhaps in five lines, again, their position, and then with full reference to all the sources but details of the sources. That is, interview with this person, that date, to be found there, paragraph so-and-so, so that the Chamber will finally be assisted in finally accepting the position of one or both parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has not received the February interviews, not from Mr. Alajica. Are they -- would they be available? And I'm not saying that they have not yet been provided, but the Chamber would like to know whether -- Yes, Mr. Markotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARKOTIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I just wanted to say that that Official Note that is being discussed was forwarded together with our report of the 23rd of February, 2009. It was forwarded to both the Chamber and the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, as I said before, the Chamber, for good reasons, has focused primarily on the submissions of the parties but has -- has exercised some self-restraint in going through all of the material which, of course, many of these -- many of these Official Notes give further information about the events at the time, and the Chamber considers it's inappropriate to -- to go around and gather whatever information there is and really wants to focus on whether what was produced satisfies the Prosecution, as far as an explanation for the non-production. Mr. Tieger, you certainly would have looked at the February -- you may be in a position to assist the Chamber in -- we'll -- of course, we'll look, perhaps now, a bit better in the boxes as well, but it is a bit disorganised material. We'll find a way to have that material available to the Chamber. Any further matter in relation to 70, 78, 80 -- 70, 71 - I apologise - 80, 81, 90, 91? In view of the time it takes, I would prefer to have an early break, and that's not to interrupt the next series. The next series, which will be 76, 77, 86, 87, 96, 97, and is about TS-5 reports to Operational Group Zadar. We'll have a break, and we will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that I announced that we would deal with 76, 77, 86, 87, and 96, 97; we'd deal with those. I referred already to the submissions, although in the wrong context. We were talking about regular reports, TS-5 for Operational Group Zadar. Reference is made to two statements of Mr. Kardum: One, 12th of February, 2009; second, 16th of March, 2009. I take it that these statements have been provided in the submissions, because the Prosecution takes the view that the statements by Mr. Kardum are contradicted by the statements by Mr. Rajcic that he had compiled written reports. Croatia's position apparently being that Rajcic describes reporting generally and not in specifics. Could I invite the parties to make further submissions in relation to this matter, which, apparently, is in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Court has already noted the -- the two contrasting information -- sources of information and pieces of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although we would like to have the details. For example, the -- we find that Mr. Rajcic contradicts which statement exactly and where to be found. We found the reference to Kardum. Could we find -- are we talking about the Rajcic statement which is -- because we find one Official Note under number 2 of the Official Notes, and I think we're talking about the -- let me just check. The filing of the 19th of January contains a list of official statements. Under number 5, is listed the note of interview with Mr. Kardum; under number 12, the statement of Mr. Rajcic. Is that what you refer to, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And just to read the relevant portion of the statement of Mr. Kardum seems to be: "Furthermore, every evening" -- and this is about Mr. Kardum, but that's the one which used in Official Notes "he," meaning Mr. Kardum: "... attended meetings at the Operational Group command, where all the subordinated commanders, including him, gave reports. He reported about weapons deployment" -- That's the passage, apparently, which -- on which the government of Croatia relies. Whereas, I see in the Rajcic statement, page 4: "In relation to the system of communication and reporting, Rajcic states that the commanders of the TS and TRS had to submit written reports two times per day, which they mostly did. The reports usually came late when the situation on the front had already changed, so there was not much use of the reports. He remembers that Milan, Gotovac, Alajica, and Mamic reported directly to the command post of the Military District to Sajkovici, that Kardum forwarded the reports through the chief of artillery of the Operations Group Zadar, Marijan First." That's what the Chamber found as apparently the most relevant sources that Croatia and the Prosecution rely upon. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: From the Prosecution's point of view, yes, Your Honour, except a note, and perhaps our colleagues from the Republic of Croatia might have noted that. I think they also rely to some accident on a 12 February 2009 Official Note from Mr. Kardum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because what I just read is a statement, 22nd of April, 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whereas, is the 12th of February to be found in the boxes? Have you received it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry the ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are referring here to the 12th of February 2009 statement. That's what we find in the footnote 53 in the -- in Appendix B which was filed on the 19th of June. Reference to a February 2009 statement which -- where can the Chamber find that? Is it -- was it produced?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I believe it was. It was not submitted with the -- obviously it wasn't submitted with the January 2009 filing by the Prosecution, nor in the June 2009, because, as I indicated before, that contained the interviews which were specifically referenced in the submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I rise because this dispute is at least partially rests on Mr. Rajcic's Official Note. I do wish to draw the Chamber's attention to the fact that Mr. Rajcic testified before this Chamber and disavowed, I would say, the majority of that Official Note including the portion relied upon by the Prosecution here, and that than disavowal begins specifically at transport page 16346, beginning at line 24. It's not clear the disavowal, but he was read the specific portion that you read, and the transcript reflects him saying: "I would never state something of the sort. And then it goes on as to why. But I did wish to note for the Chamber that the entire discussion of that Official Note begins at -- is now Exhibit P2323. The -- Mr. Rajcic's testimony on it is at 16336, beginning at line 4, to 16358, beginning at line 8. At transcript page 16350, Mr. Rajcic says the Official Note puts words in his mouth that he didn't say. So the Chamber is aware, the person that took the note, as I believe Mr. Keser who is here in Court in case there are any questions about how the note was taken. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now just for my information, we are talking about the Official Note dated the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe it's the 11th of July, 2008, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We're talking about the -- the same note of which I quoted. We here, therefore, have a double problem. Perhaps deal with the simple one, the 12th of February, 2009, Kardum interview. Mr. Tieger, where is that to be found for the Chamber? Should we dive in the boxes or -- and what box?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You have to give me a moment, Your Honour. Meanwhile and -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think we can proceed with the submissions, and we will find you an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I began by just noting the nature of that apparently conflicting information, and then I wanted to continue to note the following. And that is that Mr. Kardum says that he reported verbally to OG Zadar. That information has to go on up. One would therefore expect to find a reference to that reporting in the OG Zadar war diary. We have that diary. There are no such references that would give rise to the inference that there were some other mechanism of getting the information from the Artillery Rocket Group to the command, and the logical inference would be that -- that the normal mechanism of doing so, written reports, would be utilized. Sure enough, that's exactly what Mr. Rajcic says. So that's another of the factors that the Prosecution considers in regarding this issue as not resolved by the Kardum statement. Furthermore, this all occurs in the context of an investigation where, as previously noted, there are indications of efforts at, at least a systematic collection of the materials and documentation related to Operation Storm, the latest of which was identified on November 30th and which has recently been submitted to the Court in the Prosecution's recent filing of the correspondence. Therefore, in -- in -- and that's, I think, one of the most telling indications, and actually it signals in a number of ways a change in emphasis and information for the investigation. So in the context of an investigation where this is an indication, and increasingly strong indications, that Operation Storm documentation was systemically collected, unless the matter is more definitively resolved than this, the search should continue for information of this type and reports of this type, and that's more fulsomely the Prosecution's position on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Could I hear from the Republic of Croatia. And could your observations include comments on witnesses telling here in court that what we find in the Official Notes is not what they said, which, of course, complicates the matters, to some extent. I'm not saying who is complicating it but ... Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: One more matter, Your Honour. We will look even more carefully at the transcript, but our preliminary review of that indicates that what Mr. Misetic referred to as the Rajcic disavowal was with regard to the -- an earlier part of the -- of the note. And with respect to the portion of the note the Court read out in relation to the system of communication and reporting, Rajcic states that the commanders of the TS and TRS had to submit written reports two times per day, which they mostly did." He affirmed. So that needs to be looked at a bit more carefully, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, transcript pages, because we are not going to discuss this matter without having --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: 16346 through 47.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is not the correct transcript page, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you may both provide the transcript pages you like most, and then we will have a look at them. But let me first -- we are talking about 1634767 [sic]. And, Mr. Misetic, the competing transcript pages would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, on that specific portion, but in terms of broader context, I believe I have already read it out. The disavowal of the statement was certainly not limited to the beginning portions. I read out the -- it was 22 pages of transcript of disavowal. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And those are pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: 16336, beginning at line 4; to 16358, ending at line 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which includes the pages, you give it a broader --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- reference. Now, reading 22 pages of transcript, I will not be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I did wish to draw the Court's attention to the portion where Mr. Rajcic says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first try to get it on my screen. One second, please. Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The specific reference I made earlier, although not directly on this point, Mr. Rajcic testified at page 16350, beginning at line 1. At a different portion, this is about a part where "words are put in my mouth."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, before we continue, Mr. Markotic, I think in the -- we earlier expressed that if there would be any need to go into private session, that you could request such. I noticed that quite some of the material we're discussing at this moment were provided on a confidential basis. You, nevertheless, have not asked to go into private session. We are now dealing with transcript pages which are transcripts of testimony in private session. I just wanted to verify with you, whether you still feel at ease as matters are going now. We're not going much of detail, but at least I haven't heard any application for private session up to this moment, and I just wanted to put that on the record. I see there is no response by saying we should immediately turn into private session. So, therefore, please be aware that you always can apply for that. Now let me just ... Yes, the part I quoted earlier was read to Mr. Rajcic, and in that respect, specifically on that part, he said: "That is correct." So whatever the dispute may have been, whether it was the report accurately reflects what he said or not, that at least he agrees with this part. That is at least correct for the first part. As far as the communications and reporting system is concerned, Rajcic says that the commanders of the artillery groups and artillery rocket groups were duty-bound to send written reports twice a day, which they mostly did. This part, as he says, is correct. Then the following portion: "These reports usually came in late when the situation on the front had already changed, so that there was not much use - and I emphasise there was not much use - of the reports. He said, I would never state something of the sort, and then he explains: Every piece of information which reaches the operations centre of the main command or of the HQ, even if it is a belated one, it is, nevertheless, useful." So he says, I would not have said this because I entirely disagree, and that is the judgement on whether it was of use or not. But the first part, reporting system, and that it was mostly done, was not contested by him. I'd like to hear your submissions on both the substance but also on, Mr. Rajcic -- although perhaps not in this specific respect, distentiating [sic] himself from what is found in the Official Note, which, of course, may have consequences as far as the accuracy of the Official Notes are concerned, is concerned. Who will take the floor? Mr. Crncec, it will be you. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CRNCEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Firstly, let me point out the specific nature of Official Notes under the Law on Criminal Procedure of the Republic of Croatia. Official Notes on interviews conducted do not carry a probative value under the provisions of the Croatian criminal legislation. Secondly, we should try and establish a very important fact when discussing these specific categories of documents. Namely, the Republic of Croatia is of the opinion that, as far as the status or nature of these documents are concerned, there is disagreement between the OTP and the Republic of Croatia. That's to say, in its confidential Annex A of the submissions of the 19th of June, 2009, the OTP states that approximately 63 documents are still missing. From the filing of the 19th of January, 2009, Appendix C of the filing, these categories of documents contain footnotes 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, and 17. These footnotes state that, according to the OTP, there is insufficient information to indicate whether the document was, indeed, drafted or not. Our understanding of the matter is that in the final key of Appendix C, these categories of documents fall under the 35 categories, which were not perhaps drafted, which is something that the OTP shares as an opinion, so they would not fall under the 63 documents which, according to the OTP, are still missing. It is the view of the Republic of Croatia that the documents had not been made. This position is based on the Official Note that you, Your Honour, cited earlier on, the 12th of February, 2009 Official Note, of the interview with Mr. Kardum, commander of Artillery Group 5, who should have been the author of such a document, if it existed. The note was submitted along with the report of Croatia on the 23rd of February, 2009. The position is also based on the 16th of March, 2009, Official Note which was submitted along with Croatia's report of the 29th of April which is, again, an Official Note of an interview with Mr. Kardum, who, again, in this note, repeated that he had not kept any records or made any specific reports on the activities of his artillery group, and this is a quotation from the Official Note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, the Chamber was aware that Official Notes cannot be used as evidence in criminal proceedings. But what, in your view, is the Chamber supposed to do with Official Notes? It's clear that we cannot -- or at least that the Croatian court could not convict anyone on such a note. It could not be used as evidence. But, I mean, we have been provided with a lot of Official Notes. May I take it that there is no suggestion that we should just ignore their contents. I mean, what is the position of the Croatian government as to the accuracy of these Official Notes? Because we don't have to bother about -- primarily about the fact what a Croatian court could do with it; but what we could or could not do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CRNCEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Republic of Croatia during its administrative investigation used these Official Notes as a source of information about certain documents or facts. Therefore, we are in no position to suggest what use could be made of them by this Tribunal. We are merely pointing out the fact that some people were interviewed on several occasions, and that's been 14 years since the events in question, and that there is a possibility of seeing contradictions in their statements. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, apart from what probative value could be attached to the Official Note of an interview, 11 of July 2008, given by Mr. Rajcic, it -- it looks as if he describes different ways of reporting, Mr. Kardum this way, but he refers to others as, apparently, using other ways of reporting; that is, directly to the command post of the Military District, to Sajkovici. It seems as if Mr. Kardum says, Well, the way in which I did it, we were all together, that is how we did it; whereas, that seems not to be confirmed by Mr. Rajcic. That is, may I take it, one of the parts of what is the contradiction. Mr. Kardum reporting in a different way, and the system being described as written reports which was mostly done. Yes, Mr. Crncec.

utterances.speaker: MR. CRNCEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the quoted Official Note, Mr. Rajcic states that the commanders, for the most part, I underscore "for the most part," drafted such reports. This Official Note drafted by the competent authorities in Croatia during the administrative investigation was a starting point that was used in conducting interviews with other relevant persons; specifically, in this case, the commanders of the artillery groups who were questioned precisely about that particular thing. Mr. Kardum, on several occasions, reiterated that he never drafted written reports about the activities of his artillery group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And part of the argument of the Prosecution is that even oral reporting finds its way; it's not you listen and you forget about it, but someone would write it down in one way or another. What's your response to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KESER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Republic of Croatia, based on the information it has, states that Mr. Kardum did not report in a written form. Therefore, such information did not reach the operative group in written form. He merely stated that all that was relevant was something he noted down in his own notebook and then presented that information during briefing sessions, in terms of the activities of his artillery group. The Republic of Croatia undertook a comprehensive archival search to corroborate that fact, and I must state yet again that we have been unable to come across any traces which would prove the existence of such reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, apparently reports were made by TRS-1 to Operational Group North and TS-4 to Operational Group Sibenik. Now, would -- is that something that would be just be accepted? One commander doesn't fulfil his duty. I'm trying to understand why half of them did report; others did not. And we're all aware, isn't it, of this game played at children's parties where a message goes from one orally to the other, and we all know that, at the end of the line, the story is usually a different one from the story with which we started, which entails serious risks of mal-communication. Is there anything you would like to further say about this and about the acceptability in a hierarchical command structure? Mr. Sklepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SKLEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, while we were preparing for today's appearance before you, we envisaged a PowerPoint presentation which we were unable to show you so far. It was supposed to indicate the difference between the Operational Group and the artillery group. These forces were uneven, in terms of numbers, and they did not have the possibility to report the same way or to act in the same fashion. Given that we were unable to present it to you, and regarding your query, I can only say that the Artillery Group 5 which is being discussed, was somewhat specific, because it was at the very end, western end of the area encompassed by Operation Storm, and that the command of that group -- or, rather, commanding of that group by the Split District and its forward command post in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SKLEPIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... by Mr. Rajcic was handed over to his assistant who was within operative group Zadar. In order for one to fully grasp the existing differences - the assistant commander's name is First - he had delegated -- Mr. Rajcic had delegated that to his assistant, Mr. First after having drafted those documents together. Therefore Mr. First was in command of the artillery group itself. In order to fully appreciate the differences in question, I believe it would be of value to present that information by way of the presentation we had prepared.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The forward command post location is Sajkovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The reason why the Chamber wanted to focus on the questions rather than to receive a PowerPoint presentation is the experience that often the focus is lost if we would allow such presentations. Apart from that, there may be confusion as to the probative value of any such presentation. Whatever should be said should be already known to the Chamber, and otherwise, of course, you would appear as witnesses, and we want -- we don't want to blur these two sources of information. Now, a statement taken by Mr. First is filed on the 19th of June in Appendix C to the OTP's response to Croatia's request of the 2nd of June, 2009. Would we find the relevant information in that Official Note which was compiled 26th of March, 2009, an Official Note of an interview with Marijan First. Is that where we find the relevant information? And, if so, in which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. SKLEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the Official Note of the interview with Mr. First dated the 26th of March this year, on page 3, in the Croatian version, of course, it reads, I quote: "Once the command of Operational Group Zadar was formed," he went to the command post which was in the village of Policnik because -- sorry, where he reported to Commander Fuzul. That was probably on the 3rd of August, 1995 in the morning. With him, he brought a plan of activity of the artillery for operational group Zadar which had previously been drafted together with Mr. Rajcic. The order of the commander of the Operative Group Zadar was drafted on that occasion. He took part in the drafting of that document and created the artillery attachment to that order. He forwarded those documents to the commander of TG-5, Mr. Ante Kardum. The list of targets Jagoda was in the attachment as well as an expanded list of targets which was to be used as an auxiliary means in the course of providing artillery support. Therefore, the following can be concluded, and I have another quotation: "Concerning the system of command of the corps artillery during Operation Storm, First states that it is beyond question that the activities of all five artillery and artillery rocket groups were planned at the level of the Military District of Split." He is aware of that because he participated in it as ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I meanwhile found where are you quoting from. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SKLEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He is aware of that because he participated in it as the assistant or, rather, associate of Marko Rajcic. Concerning the implementation of the operation regarding Operative Group Zadar and the activities of TG-5, he states that he enjoyed Rajcic's trust and that Rajcic could not have physically supervised the activities of all artillery and artillery rocket groups in the entire operational area because he was focused on the activities pertaining to Knin itself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is not entirely clear to me yet to what extent the quotes you just gave justify a conclusion that there was no reporting as the reporting done by, for example, TRS-1 and TS-4. But this apparently is the matter you would think is -- you want to draw our attention to in support of your position. Anything else in relation to -- yes, Mr. Sklepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SKLEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I quoted these portions for the sole reason of showing that this artillery group enjoyed a special status, given that the chief of artillery in operative Group Zadar, Mr. First, had a special status as the first assistant to Marko Rajcic until just before that period. The reports submitted by the commander of TG-5 to Operative Group Zadar were the same as if submitted directly to the Military District of Split and Rajcic himself. The portions I quoted are from the note which provides no data about the reporting itself, but it does address the chain of command. That is my starting point when I tried to clarify our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Mr. Tieger, any submissions in relation to what was just brought to the attention of the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, except to note that those are inferences drawn from sources that don't, themselves, make the explicit connection that Mr. Sklepic just attempted to make. We didn't hear that from -- we certainly didn't hear that from Mr. Rajcic. We didn't even hear from Mr. First.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any other party or interested party to make any further submissions in relation to this group?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to complete the picture on TS-5. Another factor that we think should be kept in consideration is that Mr. Rajcic testified on the 3rd there was a change with part of TRS-5 then moving on to assist the special police. And so that -- as I'm told what was left of TRS-5 by the beginning of Operation Storm with the Split Military District was two Howitzers and two artillery pieces, and that may affect, then, why there is different reporting from other operative groups, which would have had complete sets, as opposed to what was left of TRS-5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that submission. Then we move on to my next series. Next series concern 72, 73, 82, 83, 92, 93; reporting from TS-3 to Operational Group North. The position of Croatia started by saying that the documents requested were supposed to have been drafted as requested. And at the end of the statement of the reasons, it says: "We would like to mention that, due to commanding relations, TS-3 was not even supposed to report to Operational Group North but to the forward command post, Split Military District, Sajkovici." Now, how to reconcile that the documents were supposed to have been drafted; but, at the same time, to bring to our attention that TS-3 was not even supposed to report to Operational Group North. That is not easy to understand. Could we hear from the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. SKLEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the explanation of our statement also arises from the chain of command. Operational Group North, whose commander was Rahim Ademi, was positioned -- or, rather, its command was positioned at the same location as that of forward command post of the Split Military District; namely, Sajkovici. Rahim Ademi was also commander of Operational Group North and primarily Chief of Staff of the Split Military District. He wore two hats. He had a dual role to play. Our statement that Operational Group North did not need to receive these reports to begin with arises from the very fact that these two commands were situated at the same location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You say if people are in the same location, then the mere knowledge stored in the memory of the person would do for all operational purposes. Is that the explanation? I see nodding no, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SKLEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, that that is not the explanation. I'm merely pointing out, that, according to the chain of command, the artillery group which is now being discussed, did not need to report to Operational Group North, the reporting itself, and the method of reporting is reflected in the Official Notes of interviews with Mamic and Erak of the 4th of February of this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. CRNCEC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I only quote the mentioned Official Notes? There, commander of Artillery Group 3, Mamic, stated, and I quote: "He claims that he, himself, did not write any daily reports, nor is he aware of anyone else writing them." A member of the same artillery group, Zivko Erak stated, and I quote: "On receiving an order, he stated that he used a field phone to get in touch with the positions that were supposed to open fire and related the order to them. Later on, he would report back to Sajkovici and make a note of the order in the operational diary." This was submitted to the Trial Chamber and the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I think that the documents I mentioned, a series of six, are all dealing with the same problem more or less, so, therefore, I took the explanation for 72 to include all the others as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I understood that in the same context as the earlier reviews, Your Honour. The position was that the method of reporting was reflected in the Official Notes of Mamic and Erak. It's important, therefore, to note that, in addition to what was previously asserted about Mamic's position that he didn't write any daily reports nor does he know anyone else, he was also shown, during the course of that interview, reports which he had written before Storm that had his name and indicated him as commander. And the reason he was shown that is because Mr. Mamic apparently wasn't able to remember that he was the commander. And when shown those notes which stated that he was the commander, indicated that he had written and signed them, he asserted that he was seeing for the first time. I think that bears to a large extent to the weight that can be attributed to the assertions of Mr. Mamic with respect to the reporting system in place at the time. And with respect to Mr. Erak he purported to not be aware of who his commander was. Again, Your Honour, these factors render this information insufficient to resolve this issue, particularly as I mentioned in the context of an investigation which is proceeding now with the heightened awareness that documentation regarding Storm was systematically collected and may be found elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The language in your report - and I'm now addressing the representatives of Croatia - says: "In the continuation of the operative processing, interviews were conducted with Goran Mamic and Zivko Erak. None of them confirmed that daily reports were written by the TS-3 to the superior command." That is not a firm denial that ever such reports were written, or do we have to conclude that from the context of their statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. KESER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the context of their statements, there was mention of reports from this artillery group to the superior command as part of Operation Storm. These reports were shown to Goran Mamic. They were written informally in handwriting without any reference number or class number. When it came to writing reports, he did say that he wrote them but not in relation to Operation Storm, and that's the gist of what the notes state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, part of the comments of the Office of the Prosecution was that Mr. Mamic's statement is highly unreliable because he - that's at least how I understood it - because he said that reports which bear his name in a commanding position and his signature, that he saw them for the first time, and that, as Mr. Tieger put it, he had forgotten or he didn't know anymore that he was a commander. Any comment on that aspect? Again, the Chamber has not evaluated in detail any of the Official Notes. I would say, any of the evidence, but, of course, it's at least to -- in Croatian courts, it would not be evidence, but it's material which has been made available to us to rely upon to better understand the reasons why these documents either do not exist or were not produced. Any comments on -- on what is presented by Mr. Tieger as indicia of unreliability?

utterances.speaker: MR. KESER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on the issue of Goran Mamic, it was precisely because of such statements of his that the Republic of Croatia, in an attempt to verify his assertions, spoke to his deputy, Mr. Zivko Erak, who, at the time of the implementation of Operation Storm was present at the positions along with artillery group. Whereas, Mr. Mamic was at the observation post during the operation. In other words, he was not at the HQ. Mr. Erak also stated that he had not written any sort of daily reports nor was he aware of anyone else writing them. As Mamic's deputy, he should have known if such reports were written. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the fact is that Mr. Mamic was just cited in this courtroom as the basis for the assertion with regard to those reports. One more point that should have been considered by the authorities, the Republic of Croatia, in assessing the reliability of those reports, and that is that in October of 2008, Mr. Mamic advised investigators according to that Official Note that he was a witness for the Gotovina Defence and that, as a result, prior to the interview, he had consolidations with Mr. Ivanovic who told him he could not give away the operation commanders and other details which could be detrimental to the defence of the general, by reason of which he would answer only those questions that he deemed did not present a problem and continued. Now, my recollection is that that matter was raised and disputed by the Defence. That's -- that's fine. But the point is that that's what Mr. Mamic's position was, about the information he was prepared to divulge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And about Mr. Erak? Because I think that both are mentioned as source of the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's -- Mr. Erak's position is far from definitive on that or dispositive on that issue, Your Honour, and as I say his memory was also rather faulty. But in any event he does not take a dispositive position which was the reason why it was framed as, as the deputy he would have been in a position to know. And for all the reasons stated, it cannot be said that those two statements taken together -- or interview notes taken together therefore resolve the issue in the manner suggested by the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you said Mr. Erak said that he wasn't aware who his commander was. Is that how I have to understand page 44, line 15?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, it's not entirely clear. He makes an indirect reference to -- he is anything but definitive about it. Indicates he does not know who commanded or who was supposed to command the battalion since Vlahov was not there, but he knows that his deputy Goran Mamic was at the observation post and on reconnaissance with the scouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. First, we agree entirely with the Republic of Croatia that there would have been, during operation Storm, no reason for reports to be created to Operative Group North. OG North de facto was commanded by the Split Military District directly, both because Mr. Ademi was simultaneously the Chief of Staff of the Split Military District and OG North commander. And also because they are in fact the same location. In other words OG North is being commanded from IZM Sajkovici, which is the location of the Split Military District. So it is completely false, it's our position, the Prosecution's position is untenable that such reports were drafted because it defies common sense that you would draft reports first to the OG North and then presumably OG North would send reports up the line to the Split Military District when, as a practical matter, that was not necessary. In terms of Mr. Kardum having prepared reports -- I'm sorry, in terms of reports having been prepared prior to Storm, that is because, as the Court knows from the evidence, Mr. Zdilar was the commander of OG North until he was replaced by General Ademi on the 3rd of August. So it is entirely possible and probable that reports would have been prepared from the TRS-group to the OG North command, until in essence the OG North command was wiped out prior to Operation Storm, and in its place the Split Military District Command took over direct command. That's on the first point. The Prosecution's sole argument in response is a reference to, Systematic collection of documents may be found elsewhere. I'm not sure what that's supposed to mean. There is certain innuendo in that comment, but that is certainly not any evidentiary basis, and the Prosecution has the burden here of providing actual evidence to support their claim in rebuttal that there would have been separate reports created. In this context, there is running throughout the Prosecution's argument an assertion of some sort of a conspiracy in the late 1990s, which I think that innuendo is intended to gin up again. I do believe, therefore, that the Court should consider Exhibit D1212 which is MNA status. That is the "New York Times" article from March of 1999. There, the Prosecution leaked to the international press that they had decided not to charge or not to include shelling in any indictment. And that being the case, that would certainly cut against any reason for the Croatian authorities to engage in a conspiracy to cover up artillery documents when the Office of the Prosecutor was leaking information to the "New York Times" that that was not a topic of the indictment in this case, and in fact a no-charge decision had been issued. Finally on the issue of any innuendo concerning Mr. Ivanovic, fortunately Mr. Ivanovic is here for this purpose; we brought him here in case the Chamber had any questions. I don't know what Mr. Mamic said to the Croatian authorities. We certainly challenge on the basis of Mr. Rajcic's testimony the accuracy of these Official Notes. Mr. Tieger now questions the accuracy and/or reliability of the Official Notes himself, and our position on that point was simply that people should not be giving information about how the Gotovina Defence works. That was far different from saying, You cannot talk generally about what information you knew from 1995. And to the extent that this was an issue raised at the last hearing with Croatia at the end of June which was targeting members of the Gotovina Defence or how the Gotovina Defence operates, it's our position that that goes into Rule 70(A) issues because under the work product doctrine, we are entitled to a certain amount of -- not a certain amount. We are entitled to a work product privilege. That was the extent of that issue. Certainly he was never instructed to give false information or incomplete information or anything to that effect, and we certainly wanted, as the Court is aware from last week, for this hearing to have all persons with relevant information being present --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think we're moving away now from -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And that's why Mr. Ivanovic is here, in case the Court has any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Just to fully understand, Mr. Rajcic challenged that the Official Notes reflect what he said. From what I understood, Mr. Tieger was challenging the Official Notes for a different reason. That is, that not to say that the Official Note did not reflect what Mr. Mamic had said, but that what he did say, that that was unreliable.
